Context:  Nordau begins his work with a "medical" and social interpretation of what has created this Degeneration in society. Nordau divides his study into five books. In the first book, Nordau identifies the phenomenon of fin de siĂ¨cle in Europe. He sees this as first being recognised, though not originating, in France, describing this phenomenon as "a contempt for the traditional views of custom and morality". He sees it as a sort of decadence, a world-weariness, and the wilful rejection of the moral boundaries governing the world. He uses examples from French periodicals and books in French to show how it has affected all elements of society. Nordau accuses also society of becoming more and more inclined to imitate what they see in art. He sees in the fashionable society of Paris and London that "[e]very single figure strives visibly by some singularity in outline, set, cut or colour, to startle attention violently, and imperiously to detain it. Each one wishes to create a strong nervous excitement, no matter whether agreeably or disagreeably".
Nordau establishes the cultural phenomenon of fin de siĂ¨cle in the opening pages, but he quickly moves to the viewpoint of a physician and identifies what he sees as an illness:
In the fin-de-siĂ¨cle disposition, in the tendencies of contemporary art and poetry, in the life and conduct of men who write mystic, symbolic and 'decadent' works and the attitude taken by their admirers in the tastes and aesthetic instincts of fashionable society, the confluence of two well-defined conditions of disease, with which he [the physician] is quite familiar, viz. degeneration and hysteria, of which the minor stages are designated as neurasthenia.
The book deals with numerous case studies of various artists, writers and thinkers (Oscar Wilde, Henrik Ibsen, Richard Wagner and Friedrich Nietzsche to name a few), but its basic premise remains that society and human beings themselves are degenerating, and this degeneration is both reflected in and influenced by art. Hannah Arendt, in her book The Origins of Totalitarianism, refers to late 19th Century French society as embracing unusual or exotic types or individuals, such as criminals, Gypsies and Turks, and certain others formerly not seen as socially acceptable, so Nordau's position is not novel or isolated as social criticism.
The original article's text comports quite closely to Howard Fertig, NY 1960. During the time of Nordau's writing, physical, physiognomic, or mechanical factors were still being regarded as causative in mental aberrations and malfunctions. The symbolic or mythic approached later implemented by Freud and Jung made no part of Nordau's understanding of the human psyche.

In Book I Thomas addresses Froude's claims in the early portions of The English in the West Indies. Froude's tendency to state incorrect assumptions as fact is roundly assaulted. Thomas criticizes Froude for making sweeping generalizations about the condition of blacks on multiple islands without ever talking or interacting with the people he was writing about. Thomas points out that Froude comments extensively on the lifestyles of the natives of Grenada when his only experience among the natives was peering into their houses as he rode past in a carriage. Thomas attacks many other different factual inaccuracies in Froude's work.
In Book II Thomas begins to directly address Froude's criticism of giving colonies self-rule. When Froude claims that leaders of the reform movements "did not complain that their affairs had been ill-managed" Thomas spends over two dozen pages detailing the gross abuses of power and corruption that many of the appointed governors of Trinidad have participated in. Thomas finishes the second book by refuting Froude's assertion that West Indian blacks were incredibly well taken care off by "the beneficent despotism of the English Government"

Thomas responds by accusing the West Indian governments of suppressing blacks and noting that many black intellectuals sprang up in America shortly after Emancipation because they were integrated into society. Thomas uses the examples of Fredrick Douglass and Chief Justice William Conrad Reeves extensively in his arguments about race and intelligence. Both men are black and highly successful. When Froude brings up the old stereotypes of blacks being lazy, or being cannibals or devil-worshipers, Thomas quickly counters all of the accusations. Context:  Christie's reputation as "The Queen of Crime" was built upon the large number of classic motifs that she introduced, or for which she provided the most famous example. Christie built these tropes into what is now considered classic mystery structure: a murder is committed, there are multiple suspects who are all concealing secrets, and the detective gradually uncovers these secrets over the course of the story, discovering the most shocking twists towards the end. Culprits in Christie's mysteries have included children, policemen, narrators, already deceased individuals, and sometimes comprise no known suspects (And Then There Were None) or all of the suspects (Murder on the Orient Express).
At the end, in a Christie hallmark, the detective usually gathers the surviving suspects into one room, explains the course of his deductive reasoning, and reveals the guilty party, although there are exceptions in which it is left to the guilty party to explain all (such as And Then There Were None and Endless Night, both rather nihilistic in nature).
Christie allows some culprits to escape earthly justice for a variety of reasons, such as the passage of time (retrospective cases), in which the most important characters have already died, or by active prescription. Such cases include The Witness for the Prosecution, Murder on the Orient Express, The Man in the Brown Suit, Elephants Can Remember, and The Unexpected Guest. There are instances in which a killer is not brought to justice in the legal sense but does die as a direct result of his plot, sometimes by his own hand at the direction or with the collusion of the detective (usually Hercule Poirot). This occurs in The Murder of Roger Ackroyd, Death on the Nile, Dumb Witness, Crooked House, The Hollow, The Mirror Crack'd from Side to Side, Cat Among the Pigeons, Peril at End House, Nemesis, Appointment with Death, The Secret Adversary, and Curtain. In the last of these (Curtain), no fewer than three culprits die during the course of the story.
In The A.B.C. Murders, the murderer has killed four innocent people and attempted to frame an unstable man for the crimes. Hercule Poirot, however, prevents this easy way out, ensuring a trial and hanging. In And Then There Were None, the killer's own death is intrinsic to the plot; the red herring is when and how the killer actually died. However, stage, film, and television productions of some of these mysteries were traditionally sanitized with the culprits not evading some form of justice, for a variety of reasonsÂ â e.g., censors, plot clarity, and Christie's own changing tastes. (When Christie adapted Witness for the Prosecution into a stage play, she lengthened the ending so that the murderer was also killed; this format was followed in film and television productions, most famously the Charles Laughton/Marlene Dietrich film.) In Death Comes as the End, set in ancient Egypt, the culprit is killed in the act before he can claim another victim by one of the few surviving characters.
In some stories, the question remains unresolved of whether formal justice will ever be delivered, such as Five Little Pigs and Endless Night. According to P. D. James, Christie often, but not always, made the unlikeliest character the guilty party. Savvy readers could sometimes identify the culprit by simply identifying the least likely suspect.
On an edition of Desert Island Discs in 2007, Brian Aldiss claimed that Christie had told him that she wrote her books up to the last chapter, then decided who the most unlikely suspect was, after which she would go back and make the necessary changes to "frame" that person. However, John Curran's Agatha Christie: The Secret Notebooks describes different working methods for every book in Christie's bibliography, contradicting the claim by Aldiss.

Question: In the stage version of 'Witness for the Prosecution', why did Christie change and extend the ending?

Christie extended the ending of the stage version of *Witness for the Prosecution* to ensure the murderer faced justice, as the original story allowed the culprit to escape legal consequences. This change aligned with traditional expectations of moral resolution, which were often demanded by censors and audiences. She added a twist where the murderer is killed, providing a more satisfying and punitive conclusion for the stage audience.

Context:  Set in Spain, the play deals with a conflict between two brothers over their inheritance. Don Henrique is older than Don Jamie by a year; under the system of primogeniture, Henrique is the heir to their father's estate. The late father's will gives Jamie a small income, but Henrique treats his younger brother with rudeness and condescension, breeding a hostile relationship between the two. The problem is that Henrique and his wife, Violante, have been married for a dozen years but have no children—leaving Jamie as Henrique's heir.
Jamie is a member of a circle of aristocratic friends, which includes a boy named Ascanio. The boy is the son of poor parents, but is admired for his grace and nobility of character. Among Jamie's friends is Leandro, a lusty young man who is interested in the beautiful Amaranta. She is the wife of the rapacious lawyer Bartolus; the attorney keeps his wife closely watched, and Leandro has developed a scheme to seduce her. He masquerades as a wealthy law student come to take instruction from Bartolus. The go-between in this is Lopez, the local curate and the title character.
Don Henrique, angered over Jamie's status as his heir, makes a radical move to change the situation: he files a legal suit (Bartolus is his lawyer) to have the boy Ascanio declared his heir. Henrique testifies that before he married Violante, he was engaged or "precontracted" to Ascanio's mother Jacinta, and that the boy is his natural son. (Like other plays of the era, The Spanish Curate exploits the legal and ethical ambiguity of the precontract, which in some interpretations was like a demi-marriage...but not quite.) After the child's birth, Henrique had second thoughts about the social gap between himself and Jacinta, and got the precontract cancelled. Jacinta can only affirm the basic truth of Henrique's testimony; and on that basis, Henrique wins his suit. Ascanio is now his legal heir, and Jamie is out.
Violante, however, is outraged that Henrique has exposed this shameful affair and effectively thrown her infertility in her face. She bullies her husband into reversing course and driving Ascanio out of his house; Henrique offers the boy financial support, but the child returns to Jacinta and his pretended father Octavio. Violante is not satisfied with this, however; she reveals herself to be a truly ruthless person when she solicits Jamie to murder both Henrique and Ascanio and so come into his family fortune immediately.
Leandro works his way into the trust of Bartolus, and tries to seduce Amaranta; she is tempted by him, but stands on her virtue and fidelity. When Bartolus finally becomes suspicious, Amaranta can show that she and Leandro have been in church, and not having a sexual assignation.
The plot comes to a head in the final act: Violante meets Jamie and his pretended accomplices for the double murder—only to have her plot exposed. Henrique is shocked into penitence by the exposure of his wife's murder plot—and reveals that he and Violante are not actually, fully legally, married after all. Bartolus too is cowed by his involvement in the matter, and vows to change his ways. Jamie has no problem accepting Ascanio as his nephew, now that their family relations are better ordered. Massinger ends the play with a couplet extolling the middle way in marital relations, between too much pliability in a husband (like Henrique) and too little (like Bartolus)—much like the concluding couplet in Massinger's later play The Picture.

Context:  Set almost a decade after Rainbow Valley, Europe is on the brink of the First World War, and Anne's youngest daughter Rilla is an irrepressible almost-15-year-old, excited about her first adult party and blissfully unaware of the chaos that the Western world is about to enter. (In an aside, it is revealed that Marilla has died; her date of death is not specified but Rilla states it was before she was old enough to know her very well.)
Once the Continent descends into war, Jem Blythe and Jerry Meredith promptly enlist, upsetting Anne, Nan, and Faith Meredith (who Rilla suspects is engaged to Jem). Rilla's brother Walter, who is of age, does not enlist, ostensibly due to a recent bout with typhoid but truly because he fears the ugliness of war and death. He confides in Rilla that he feels he is a coward.
The enlisted boys report to Kingsport for training. Jem's dog, Dog Monday, takes up a vigil at the Glen train station waiting for Jem to come back. Rilla's siblings Nan, Di, and Walter return to Redmond College, and Shirley returns to Queen's Academy, leaving Rilla anxiously alone at home with her parents, their spinster housekeeper Susan Baker, and Gertrude Oliver, a teacher who is boarding with the Blythes while her fiance reports to the front.
As the war drags on, Rilla matures, organizing the Junior Red Cross in her village. While collecting donations for the war effort, she comes across a house where a young mother has just died with her husband away at war, leaving no one to care for her two-week-old son. Rilla takes the sickly little boy back to Ingleside in a soup tureen, naming him "James Kitchener Anderson" after his father and Herbert Kitchener, British Secretary of State for War. Rilla's father Gilbert challenges her to raise the war orphan, and although she doesn't like babies at all, she rises to the occasion, eventually coming to love "Jims" as her own. Walter eventually does enlist, as does Rilla's newfound love interest, Kenneth Ford (the son of Owen and Leslie Ford, who met in Anne's House of Dreams), who kisses her before leaving and asks her to promise she will not kiss anyone else until he returns. Context:  After a stirring opening on the eve of the coup d'état, involving an idealistic young village couple joining up with the republican militia in the middle of the night, Zola then spends the next few chapters going back in time to pre-Revolutionary Provence, and proceeds to lay the foundations for the entire Rougon-Macquart cycle, committing himself to what would become the next twenty-two years of his life's work. The fictional town of Plassans (loosely based on the real city of Aix-en-Provence, where Zola grew up) is established as the setting for the novel and described in intimate detail, and then we are introduced to the eccentric heroine Adelaide Fouque, later known as "Tante Dide", who becomes the common ancestor for both the Rougon and Macquart families. Her legitimate son from her short marriage to her late husband, a labourer named Rougon who worked on Dide's land, is forced to grow up alongside two illegitimate children — a boy and a girl — from Dide's later romance with the smuggler, poacher and alcoholic Macquart, while the ageing Dide slides further and further into a state of mental illness and borderline senile dementia. From this premise, the next nineteen novels all get their central protagonists and to a certain extent their themes.
The narrative continues along double lines, following both "branches" of the family. We see Pierre Rougon (the legitimate son) in his attempts to disinherit his Macquart half-siblings, his marriage to Felicité Puech, the voraciously ambitious daughter of a local merchant, and their continued failure to establish the fortune, fame and renown they seek, despite their greed and relatively comfortable lifestyles. Approaching old age, the Rougon couple finally admit defeat and settle, crushed, into their lower middle class destinies, until by a remarkable stroke of luck their eldest son Eugène reports from Paris that he has some news that they might find interesting. Eugène has become one of the closest allies of the future Emperor Napoleon III and informs his parents that a coup is imminent. Having been effectively given insider information about which side to back in the coming revolution, the Rougons then make a series of seemingly bold moves to show their loyal and steadfast support for Napoleon III, winning the admiration of the most influential people in the town, mostly royalists who are themselves afraid of showing too much commitment for fear of backing the "wrong horse" and losing their standing and fortune.
The narrative then switches over to the Macquart side of the family, whose grim working-class struggles to survive are juxtaposed keenly with the Rougons' seemingly trivial quest for greater wealth and influence in genteel drawing-room society. Descended from a drunken ne'er-do-well and a madwoman, Zola effectively predestines the Macquarts to lives of toil and misery. Zola's theories of heredity, laid out in the original preface to this novel, were a cornerstone of his entire philosophy and a major reason for his embarking on the mammoth Rougon-Macquart project in the first place in order to illustrate them. Largely discredited nowadays, the theories are largely "present but unseen" in most of the novels in the Rougon-Macquart cycle, allowing those books to be enjoyed without the overshadowing effect of Zola's somewhat suspect scientific ideas. Due to the original story nature of La Fortune des Rougon, the theories are placed much more to the fore, and can appear somewhat heavy-handed as a result.
A third branch of the family, the Mourets, descended from Macquart and Dide's daughter, are then introduced before the novel's focus is brought back to the "present", the night of the coup, via a quite brilliantly told love story. The idealistic but naïve Silvère Mouret falls madly in love with the innocent Miette Chantegreil, and after a long courtship they decide to join up with the republicans to fight the coup. The rest of the novel then picks up from where the opening chapter left off, and from then on is basically a dual narrative telling the story of the old Rougon couple and their increasingly Machiavellian machinations to get themselves into a position of fortune and respect in Plassans, juxtaposed with Silvère and Miette's continuing love story and the doomed republican militia's disastrous attempt to take the town back. Eventually, the Rougons exploit their half-brother Antoine Macquart into inadvertently helping crush the republican threat, and they achieve their life's ambition, fortune and favour. For Silvère and Miette, who committed themselves so completely to a doomed cause, there can be no such happy ending and Zola wisely leaves their half of the story at a bleak dead end..

```python
from typing import List

def isAcronym(words: List[str], s: str) -> bool:
    # If the length of words is different from the length of s,
    # s cannot be the acronym.
    if len(words) != len(s):
        return False
    
    # Construct the acronym by concatenating the first character of each word
    # and compare it with s.
    acronym = "".join(word[0] for word in words)
    return acronym == s
```

Therefore the days are naturally divided into **segments** – maximal continuous
substrings that contain no `0`.  
Inside one segment a T‑shirt cannot be reused, but after a `0` all T‑shirts are
clean again and can be used in the next segment.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 1.   What is needed inside one segment ?

For a segment let  

* `c1` – number of `1`’s (meal days)  
* `c2` – number of `2`’s (competition days)

We have `M` plain T‑shirts.  
In this segment at most `M` of the meals can be covered with plain shirts,
the remaining meals need a logo shirt.

```
logo needed for meals = max(0, c1 - M)
logo needed for competitions = c2
total logo shirts needed in this segment = c2 + max(0, c1 - M)
```

All those logo shirts have to be *different* inside the segment, otherwise a
shirt would be used twice without washing.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 2.   How many logo shirts must be bought ?

The same set of logo shirts can be reused in different segments (they are washed
on every `0`).  
Hence we only have to own enough logo shirts for the **worst** segment.

```
answer = max over all segments ( c2 + max(0, c1 - M) )
```

If the string consists only of `0`’s there is no segment and the answer is `0`.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 3.   Algorithm
```
read N, M and the string S
max_need = 0
c1 = c2 = 0                     # counters for the current segment

for each character ch in S:
    if ch == '0':
        # segment finished – evaluate it
        need = c2 + max(0, c1 - M)
        max_need = max(max_need, need)
        c1 = c2 = 0             # start a new segment
    else if ch == '1':
        c1 += 1
    else:                       # ch == '2'
        c2 += 1

# last segment (if the string does not end with '0')
need = c2 + max(0, c1 - M)
max_need = max(max_need, need)

print(max_need)
```

`N ≤ 1000`, the loop is `O(N)` time and `O(1)` memory.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 4.   Correctness Proof  

We prove that the algorithm outputs the minimum number of logo T‑shirts that
must be bought.

---

##### Lemma 1  
For any segment with `c1` meals and `c2` competitions, at least  
`c2 + max(0, c1 - M)` distinct logo shirts are necessary.

**Proof.**  
*All* competition days need a logo shirt ⇒ at least `c2` distinct logos.  
Only `M` plain shirts exist, therefore at most `M` meals can be covered by plain
shirts. If `c1 > M`, the remaining `c1-M` meals also need logo shirts, each
different because shirts cannot be reused inside the segment.  
Thus the total lower bound is `c2 + max(0, c1-M)`. ∎



##### Lemma 2  
If we own `L` logo shirts with  

```
L ≥ c2 + max(0, c1 - M)
```

for a given segment, then the segment can be processed without violating any
rule.

**Proof.**  
Give a distinct logo shirt to every competition day (`c2` shirts).  
If `c1 ≤ M`, all meals can be covered by plain shirts, no logo needed.  
If `c1 > M`, assign plain shirts to any `M` meals, and give a distinct
remaining logo shirt to each of the other `c1-M` meals.  
All used logo shirts are distinct, their total number is exactly
`c2 + (c1-M) = c2 + max(0, c1-M) ≤ L`.  Hence feasible. ∎



##### Lemma 3  
Let  

```
need = max over all segments ( c2 + max(0, c1 - M) )
```

Owning `need` logo shirts is sufficient for the whole schedule.

**Proof.**  
Consider any segment. By definition of `need`,
`need ≥ c2 + max(0, c1 - M)` for this segment.  
Apply Lemma 2 with `L = need` ⇒ the segment can be processed.
Since after every `0` all shirts are washed, the same `need` logo shirts can be
reused for every segment. ∎



##### Lemma 4  
Any feasible solution needs at least `need` logo shirts.

**Proof.**  
Take the segment that attains the maximum in the definition of `need`.  
By Lemma 1 that segment alone requires at least
`c2 + max(0, c1 - M) = need` distinct logo shirts.
Therefore any feasible overall solution must own at least `need` logo shirts. ∎



##### Theorem  
The algorithm outputs the minimum possible number of logo T‑shirts to buy.

**Proof.**  
The algorithm computes `max_need`, which is exactly the value `need`
defined above.  
* By Lemma 3, `max_need` logo shirts are sufficient → the algorithm’s
  output is feasible.
* By Lemma 4, no solution can use fewer than `max_need` logo shirts →
  the output is optimal.

Thus the algorithm returns the minimum required number. ∎



--------------------------------------------------------------------

```python
def solve() -> None:
    data = sys.stdin.read().strip().split()

    N = int(data[0])
```

To solve this problem efficiently, we need to determine whether adding a new edge to a graph preserves a certain "goodness" property.

### Problem Understanding:
- We are given a graph $ G $ with $ N $ vertices and $ M $ edges.
- A graph is **good** if, for each of the $ K $ specified pairs $ (x_i, y_i) $, there is **no path** between $ x_i $ and $ y_i $ in the graph.
- Initially, the graph $ G $ is good.
- We are given $ Q $ queries. Each query adds an edge $ (p_i, q_i) $ to the graph and asks: **Is the resulting graph still good?**

### Key Ideas:
1. We need to determine connectivity in the original graph. This naturally suggests using **Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union, DSU)**.
2. Initially, run DSU on the given $ M $ edges. This will group the vertices into connected components.
3. For each forbidden pair $ (x_i, y_i) $, we **must ensure** that $ x_i $ and $ y_i $ are **not in the same component**, which they aren't initially.
4. When we add a new edge $ (p, q) $, we are potentially connecting two components.
   - If adding $ (p, q) $ **connects any previously disconnected forbidden pair $ (x_i, y_i) $**, then the graph is no longer good.
   - But note: we don’t have to simulate every query independently — instead, we can **precompute** which component each vertex belongs to initially.

### Plan:
- Use DSU to compute connected components of the original graph.
- For each forbidden pair $ (x_i, y_i) $, record that $ x_i $ and $ y_i $ **must remain disconnected**. So if they are already connected in the base graph, input ensures they aren’t (given as good).
- However, if the added edge connects two components such that a forbidden pair becomes connected, answer is `No`.
- But here’s the key: **adding an edge merges two components.**
  - So, suppose we merge components $ C_p $ and $ C_q $. Then any vertex in $ C_p $ becomes connected to any vertex in $ C_q $.
  - Therefore, if **any forbidden pair** has one vertex in $ C_p $ and the other in $ C_q $, then adding this edge would violate the condition.

### How to efficiently check this?
- We cannot check all $ K $ pairs for each query (too slow: $ O(QK) $).
- Alternate idea: **compress the forbidden pairs by components**.
  - Let’s assign each vertex its root (component id) via DSU.
  - For each forbidden pair $ (x, y) $, we get the components: $ \text{root}_x $, $ \text{root}_y $. Without loss of generality, store this pair in sorted order.
  - Now, maintain a **set of forbidden component pairs**: $ (\min(r_x, r_y), \max(r_x, r_y)) $ for each $ (x, y) $.

Then for each query $ (p, q) $:
- Find their roots $ r_p $, $ r_q $. If they are already in the same component → adding this edge does **nothing** → so the graph remains good (`Yes`).
- Else, check if $ (\min(r_p, r_q), \max(r_p, r_q)) $ is present in the forbidden component pairs.
  - If **yes**, then this edge connects two components that contain a forbidden pair → graph becomes bad → `No`.
  - If **no**, then this merge doesn’t cause any forbidden connection → remains good → `Yes`.

### Implementation Steps:
1. Read input.
2. Use DSU to build connected components from the $ M $ edges.
3. Normalize all vertex roots (using find).
4. Build a set of forbidden component pairs $ (r_x, r_y) $ (sorted).
5. For each query:
   - Get roots of $ p_i $, $ q_i $
   - If roots are equal → already connected → no new connection → safe → `Yes`
   - Else, check if $ (\min(r_p, r_q), \max(r_p, r_q)) $ is in the forbidden set → if yes, print `No`, else `Yes`

```python
import sys

def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split()
    it = iter(data)
    
    N = int(next(it)); M = int(next(it))
    
    parent = list(range(N+1))
    rank = [0] * (N+1)
    
    def find(x):
        if parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = find(parent[x])
        return parent[x]
    
    def union(x, y):
        rx = find(x)
        ry = find(y)
        if rx == ry:
            return
        if rank[rx] < rank[ry]:
            parent[rx] = ry
        elif rank[rx] > rank[ry]:
            parent[ry] = rx
        else:
            parent[ry] = rx
            rank[rx] += 1
    
    for _ in range(M):
        u = int(next(it)); v = int(next(it))
        union(u, v)
    
    # Normalize all roots
    for i in range(1, N+1):
        find(i)
    
    K = int(next(it))
    forbidden_component_pairs = set()
    
    for _ in range(K):
        x = int(next(it)); y = int(next(it))
        rx = find(x)
        ry = find(y)
        if rx > ry:
            rx, ry = ry, rx
        forbidden_component_pairs.add((rx, ry))
    
    Q = int(next(it))
    out_lines = []
    
    for _ in range(Q):
        p = int(next(it)); q = int(next(it))
        rp = find(p)
        rq = find(q)
        if rp == rq:
            # Already in same component, no new connection
            out_lines.append("Yes")
        else:
            if rp > rq:
                rp, rq = rq, rp
            if (rp, rq) in forbidden_component_pairs:
                out_lines.append("No")
            else:
                out_lines.append("Yes")
    
    print("\n".join(out_lines))

main()
```

- If so, answer `No`; else, `Yes`.

- $ O(M \alpha(N)) $ for DSU

For every cell we know its colour  

* `#` – green  
* `.` – red  

Let

We choose one red cell uniformly, repaint it green and look at the new
number of green components `C`.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 1.   Effect of repainting one cell  

For a fixed red cell `v`

* look at its four orthogonal neighbours,
* among them consider only the green ones,
* let `k(v)` be the number of **different** green components that appear
  among those neighbours.

```
k(v) = 0   :   no green neighbour
k(v) >= 1 :   neighbour cells belong to k(v) distinct components
```

Repainting `v`

* if `k(v) = 0` – a new isolated green component appears  

  `C = C0 + 1`
* otherwise – the `k(v)` neighbour components become merged together
  with the new cell, i.e. `k(v)` components are replaced by one  

  `C = C0 - (k(v) - 1) = C0 + 1 - k(v)`

Both cases are expressed by the same formula  

```
C(v) = C0 + 1 - k(v)            (1)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 2.   Expected value  

The expected value over all red cells is

```
E = ( Σ_{red v} C(v) ) / R
  = ( Σ (C0 + 1 - k(v)) ) / R
  = C0 + ( Σ (1 - k(v)) ) / R                     (2)
```

All we have to know is  

* `C0` – total green components in the original grid,
* for every red cell `v` the number `k(v)` of distinct neighbour
  components,
* `R` – number of red cells.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 3.   Computing `C0` and the component id of each green cell  

We run a **BFS/DFS** over the whole grid, visiting only green cells.
Every discovered component receives a new id (`1,2,…`).  
While doing that we also store for each cell `comp[i][j]`  

* `0`  – the cell is red,
* `>0` – id of the green component it belongs to.

Complexities  

* time   `O(H·W)` – each cell processed once,
* memory `O(H·W)` integers (`≤ 10⁶`, well inside limits).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 4.   Computing `k(v)` for every red cell  

For each red cell we inspect its up to four neighbours,
collect the component ids that are `>0` into a small set
(at most four elements).  
`k(v)` = size of that set.

While iterating over all red cells we accumulate  

```
S = Σ (1 - k(v))          (may be negative)
```

All operations are performed modulo `MOD = 998244353`.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 5.   Final formula modulo `MOD`

From (2)

```
answer = C0 + S / R   (mod MOD)
```

Division modulo a prime is multiplication by the modular inverse:

```
invR = R^(MOD-2)  (Fermat)
answer = ( C0 + S * invR ) mod MOD
```

`C0` is at most `H·W ≤ 10⁶`, fits into normal integers.

We prove that the algorithm prints the required value.

adjacent to `v`. After repainting `v` green the total number of green

If `k(v)=0` the new cell is isolated → one new component, total `C0+1`.

##### Lemma 3  
The BFS/DFS labeling performed by the algorithm assigns a unique id to
every green connected component and no two different components receive
the same id.

**Proof.**  
The search starts from an unvisited green cell, explores all reachable
green cells using only edges between orthogonal neighbours – exactly the

##### Lemma 4

```python
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def sumOfPower(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        MOD = 10**9 + 7
        # Sort the array to easily determine min and max for subsets
        nums.sort()
        
        ans = 0
        # min_sum represents the sum of minimums of all non-empty subsets 
        # formed by the elements processed so far.
        min_sum = 0
        
        for x in nums:
            # The contribution of x as the maximum element of a group.
            # The group must contain x. The other elements can be any subset of the 
            # previously seen elements (which are all smaller than x).
            # The power formula is max^2 * min.
            # Here max is x.
            # The sum of (min) for all valid groups is (min_sum + x).
            # +x accounts for the group containing only {x}.
            # min_sum accounts for groups formed by taking any non-empty subset of 
            # previous elements (which contributes its min) and adding x to it.
            
            term_sq = (x * x) % MOD
            term_min = (min_sum + x) % MOD
            contribution = (term_sq * term_min) % MOD
            
            ans = (ans + contribution) % MOD
            
            # Update min_sum for the next iteration.
            # If the current set of elements is S, new set is S U {x}.
            # The sum of mins for S U {x} is:
            # Sum(min(subset)) for subset in S (Part A)
            # + Sum(min(subset U {x})) for subset in S (Part B)
            # Since x is greater than all elements in S, min(subset U {x}) is min(subset) if subset is not empty,
            # and x if subset is empty.
            # So Part B is (Sum(min(subset)) for non-empty subset in S) + x
            # This is just min_sum + min_sum + x = 2 * min_sum + x.
            min_sum = (min_sum * 2 + x) % MOD
            
        return ans
```

**Solution Explanation**

For every event  

* `t = 1 , x` – a potion of type `x` is found.  
  We may **take** it (`+1` potion in the bag) or **discard** it.  

* `t = 2 , x` – a monster of type `x` appears.  
  We **must** use one potion of the same type that we have already taken,
  otherwise we lose.

`N ≤ 2·10⁵`.

For a feasible strategy we have to decide for every *supply* event (`t = 1`)
whether we take the potion or not.
All monsters have to be defeated.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 1.   Observations  

*Only the *number* of taken potions matters for the size of the bag.*

Let  

* `pick(i)`   – number of taken potions among the first `i` events,
* `dem(i)`   – number of monsters among the first `i` events  
  (every monster is necessarily defeated).

Then the number of potions in the bag **after** event `i` is  

```
bag(i) = pick(i) – dem(i)
```

`dem(i)` is fixed, therefore the peaks of the bag are caused only by
`pick(i)`.  
We want a feasible set of taken supplies such that the maximum of
`pick(i) – dem(i)` becomes as small as possible.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 2.   When does a supply have to be taken?  

Look at one concrete type `c`.  
Consider its events in chronological order, e.g.

```
... 1 c   1 c   2 c   1 c   2 c   2 c   ...
```

Every monster (`2 c`) needs a *previous* supply (`1 c`) that we have taken.
If we already know which supplies will be used for the monsters,
the other supplies may be discarded.

**Greedy rule (per type)**  

When a monster of type `c` appears, match it with the **latest**
still unused supply of the same type that happened before the monster.

Why is “latest” optimal?

*The potion is kept in the bag only between the moment we take it and the
moment we consume it.  
Using the latest possible supply shortens this interval, therefore it can
only decrease (or keep equal) the maximal number of potions that are
still unused at any time.*

Consequently, for every type independently this rule yields a feasible
matching that minimises the number of *active* (taken but not yet used)
potions at every moment.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 3.   Whole algorithm  

All types are independent, therefore we can apply the rule simultaneously.

```
for each type c                     // a stack of still unused supplies
    stack[c] = empty

need[i] = 0   (i = 0 … N‑1)           // will be 1 iff we must take this supply

scan events i = 0 … N‑1
    if t[i] == 1                     // a supply of type x
          push i onto stack[x]
    else                               // a monster of type x
          if stack[x] is empty        // no earlier supply → impossible
                 output -1 and finish
          idx = pop from stack[x]     // latest unused supply of this type
          need[idx] = 1               // we must take it
```

If the scan finishes, a feasible strategy exists.
All supplies marked `need = 1` are taken, the others are discarded.
The matching created by the pops guarantees that every monster can be
defeated.

Now we compute the minimal possible peak `K_min`.

```
pick = 0            // taken so far
dem  = 0            // monsters so far
Kmax = 0

scan events i = 0 … N‑1
    if t[i] == 1
          if need[i] == 1:   pick += 1
    else
          dem += 1
    Kmax = max(Kmax, pick - dem)
K_min = Kmax
```

`K_min` is exactly the smallest possible maximal bag size,
because any feasible strategy must take at least the supplies selected
by the greedy matching (otherwise some monster would lack a potion),
and the greedy matching yields the smallest possible number of simultaneously
active potions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 4.   Correctness Proof  

We prove that the algorithm outputs `-1` iff survival is impossible,
otherwise it outputs the correct `K_min` and a strategy that achieves it.

---

##### Lemma 1  
For a fixed potion type `c`, let the algorithm match each monster to the
latest previously unmatched supply of that type.
Among all ways to assign supplies of type `c` to its monsters,
this assignment minimises, for every moment,
the number of taken but not yet used supplies of type `c`.

**Proof.**  
Consider any monster `M` of type `c` occurring at position `p`.
Let `S` be the supply chosen by the algorithm (the latest unused before `p`).
Any other feasible assignment must give `M` a supply `S'` that appears
before `p` and is unused at that time.
If `S'` is earlier than `S`, then the interval `[S', p]` strictly contains
`[S, p]`.  
Therefore at every moment the set of active supplies under the algorithm
is a subset of the active supplies under any other assignment.
∎



##### Lemma 2  
If the algorithm finishes the scan without outputting `-1`,
the set `need = 1` is sufficient to defeat every monster.

**Proof.**  
When a monster of type `c` is processed, the algorithm pops a prior supply
of the same type and marks it `need = 1`.  
Thus, for that monster there exists a distinct earlier supply that will be
taken.  
Different monsters pop different supplies (they are removed from the stack),
so each monster gets its own potion. ∎



##### Lemma 3  
If the algorithm outputs `-1`, then no strategy can defeat all monsters.

**Proof.**  
`-1` is printed exactly when a monster of type `c` appears while the stack
for `c` is empty, i.e. there is no earlier supply of type `c` at all.
Because a potion can only be taken at a supply event, any strategy would
have zero potions of this type before the monster, hence the monster cannot
be defeated. ∎



##### Lemma 4  
Let `need` be the set produced by the algorithm (when it does not output `-1`).
For any feasible strategy `S`, let `pick_S(i)` be the number of taken supplies
among the first `i` events.
Then for every `i`  

```
pick(i) ≤ pick_S(i)
```

where `pick(i)` is the number of supplies with `need = 1` among the first `i`
events.

**Proof.**  
Consider an arbitrary type `c`.  
By Lemma 1 the algorithm uses the latest possible supplies for the
monsters of this type, therefore at any prefix the algorithm has taken the
*minimum* number of supplies of type `c` that is still enough to satisfy the
monsters of that type appearing inside the prefix.
Any feasible overall strategy must have at least this many supplies of type
`c` in the same prefix (otherwise some monster of type `c` would be lacking a
potion).  
Summation over all types gives the inequality for the total number of taken
supplies. ∎



##### Lemma 5  
Let `K_min` be the value printed by the algorithm.
For every feasible strategy the maximal bag size is at least `K_min`.

**Proof.**  
For any feasible strategy `S` and any position `i`

```
bag_S(i) = pick_S(i) – dem(i)
```

By Lemma 4  `pick(i) ≤ pick_S(i)`, therefore

```
bag_S(i) ≥ pick(i) – dem(i)
```

Taking the maximum over all positions yields

```
max_i bag_S(i) ≥ max_i (pick(i) – dem(i)) = K_min .
```
∎



##### Lemma 6  
The strategy defined by `need` (take exactly those supplies) attains a
maximal bag size equal to `K_min`.

**Proof.**  
During the scan that computes `K_min` we exactly simulate this strategy:
`pick` counts the supplies with `need = 1`,
`dem` counts monsters.
`K_max` is the maximum of `pick – dem`, i.e. the maximal bag size of the
strategy. By definition `K_max = K_min`. ∎



##### Theorem  
The algorithm

* prints `-1` **iff** it is impossible to defeat all monsters,
* otherwise prints the minimal possible maximal bag size `K_min`,
  and a list of actions (for each supply event) that achieves it.

**Proof.**  

*If the algorithm prints `-1`*: by Lemma 3 survival is impossible.  

*If the algorithm finishes*:  
  - By Lemma 2 the produced actions defeat every monster, so a feasible
    strategy exists.  
  - Lemma 6 shows that the printed actions achieve a maximal bag size
    `K_min`.  
  - Lemma 5 shows that no feasible strategy can have a smaller maximal
    bag size.  

Thus `K_min` is optimal and the printed actions are valid. ∎



--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 5.   Complexity Analysis  

*Stacks*: one list per type, total `N` pushes and pops.  

*Scanning*: two linear passes over the `N` events.

```
Time   :  O(N)
Memory :  O(N)          // the `need` array and the stacks
```

Both satisfy the limits (`N ≤ 2·10⁵`).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 6.   Reference Implementation  (Python 3)

```python
import sys

def solve() -> None:
    it = iter(sys.stdin.read().strip().split())
    try:
        N = int(next(it))
    except StopIteration:
        return
    t = [0] * N
    x = [0] * N
    for i in range(N):
        t[i] = int(next(it))
        x[i] = int(next(it))

    # stacks for each type (1‑based)
    stacks = [[] for _ in range(N + 1)]
    need = [0] * N                     # 1 if we must take this supply

    for i in range(N):
        if t[i] == 1:                  # supply
            stacks[x[i]].append(i)     # remember its index
        else:                          # monster
            typ = x[i]
            if not stacks[typ]:        # no earlier supply of this type
                print(-1)
                return
            idx = stacks[typ].pop()    # latest unused supply
            need[idx] = 1              # we have to take it

    # compute K_min
    pick = 0
    dem = 0
    Kmax = 0
    for i in range(N):
        if t[i] == 1:
            if need[i]:
                pick += 1
        else:
            dem += 1
        cur = pick - dem
        if cur > Kmax:
            Kmax = cur

    # output
    out = []
    out.append(str(Kmax))
    # second line: actions for each supply event in order
    actions = [str(need[i]) for i in range(N) if t[i] == 1]
    out.append(' '.join(actions))
    sys.stdout.write('\n'.join(out))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    solve()
```

```python
    max_sum = sum(nums)
    
    # Initialize DP array. dp[s] stores the number of ways to form sum s.
    # dp[0] = 1 (empty multiset)

        # This multiplies the number of ways to achieve sum s by (zero_count + 1).
        for i in range(max_sum + 1):
            dp[i] = dp[i] * (zero_count + 1) % MOD
        del freq[0]
        
    # Process each unique value and its count
    for val, cnt in freq.items():
        # Create a copy of the current DP state to store the new state
        new_dp = dp[:]

        # to use a sliding window technique for bounded knapsack
```

**Solution Explanation**

For every sub‑array `nums[i … j]` let  

```
d(i,j) = number of distinct values in that sub‑array
```

The *uniqueness array* is the multiset  

```
U = { d(i,j) | 0 ≤ i ≤ j < n }
```

`|U| = n·(n+1)/2`.  
The required answer is the median of `U`, i.e. the smallest value `x`
such that at least half of the elements of `U` are `≤ x`.

The problem therefore reduces to the following decision question:

> **Given a value `x`, how many sub‑arrays have at most `x` distinct
> values?**

If we can answer this in `O(n)` we can binary‑search `x` in the range
`[1, n]` (the number of distinct elements in any sub‑array cannot exceed the
array length).  
Overall complexity `O(n log n)` and `O(1)` extra memory.



--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 1.   Counting sub‑arrays with ≤ x distinct elements  

We use the classic two‑pointer (sliding window) technique.

```
left  = 0
freq  = empty hash map   // value -> occurrences inside current window
distinct = 0
cnt = 0                  // answer for the current x

for right from 0 to n-1:
        add nums[right] to freq
        if its frequency becomes 1: distinct += 1

        while distinct > x:
                remove nums[left] from freq
                if its frequency becomes 0: distinct -= 1
                left += 1

        // now window [left … right] has ≤ x distinct elements
        // all sub‑arrays ending at `right` and starting anywhere between
        // left and right are valid → there are (right‑left+1) of them
        cnt += right - left + 1
```

`cnt` is exactly the number of sub‑arrays whose distinct count does **not**
exceed `x`. The loop runs `n` times, each element is added once and removed
once → `O(n)` time, `O(number of different values)` map size, i.e. `O(n)` in
the worst case, but only `O(1)` extra *algorithmic* memory besides the hash
map.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 2.   Binary search for the median  

```
total = n·(n+1)//2
need  = (total + 1) // 2          // index of the median (1‑based)

lo = 1
hi = n
while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if count_subarrays_with_at_most(mid) >= need:
                hi = mid            // median ≤ mid
        else:
                lo = mid + 1        // median > mid
return lo
```

The predicate is monotone: if a certain `mid` already gives at least `need`
sub‑arrays, any larger `mid` will also satisfy it. Therefore binary search
finds the smallest `mid` with the property, which by definition is the
median (the “smaller of the two middle values” rule is automatically fulfilled
by taking the leftmost feasible value).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 3.   Correctness Proof  

We prove that the algorithm returns the required median.

---

##### Lemma 1  
For any integer `x (1 ≤ x ≤ n)`, the procedure `count_subarrays_with_at_most(x)`
returns the number of sub‑arrays whose distinct element count is **≤ x**.

**Proof.**  
The sliding‑window invariant after the inner `while` finishes is  
`distinct ≤ x` for the window `[left … right]`.  
Every sub‑array that ends at `right` and starts at an index `s` with
`left ≤ s ≤ right` is a sub‑array of this window, hence also has  
`distinct ≤ x`. There are exactly `right‑left+1` such starts, which we add to
`cnt`. No other sub‑array ending at `right` can satisfy the condition,
because any start `< left` would make the window contain more than `x`
distinct values (the `while` would not have terminated).  
Processing all `right` from `0` to `n‑1` enumerates *all* sub‑arrays, each
exactly once, and adds `1` precisely when its distinct count ≤ x. ∎



##### Lemma 2  
Define  

```
F(x) = number of sub‑arrays with distinct count ≤ x
```

Then `F` is monotone non‑decreasing in `x`.

**Proof.**  
If a sub‑array has ≤ x distinct values, it also has ≤ (x+1) distinct values.
Thus the set counted for `x` is a subset of the set counted for `x+1`. ∎



##### Lemma 3  
Let `need = (total+1)//2`.  
The smallest integer `m` with `F(m) ≥ need` equals the median of the
uniqueness array (with the “smaller of the two middle values” rule).

**Proof.**  
The uniqueness array sorted increasingly contains `total` elements.
The median definition required here is the element at position `need`
(1‑based). By definition of `F`, for any value `v` the number of elements
≤ v in the sorted uniqueness array is exactly `F(v)`. The smallest `v`
with at least `need` elements not larger than it is precisely the element
at position `need`. ∎



##### Lemma 4  
The binary search returns the smallest `m` such that `F(m) ≥ need`.

**Proof.**  
Binary search maintains the invariant that the answer lies in `[lo, hi]`
and that `F(lo‑1) < need` (if `lo>1`) and `F(hi) ≥ need`.

```python
    Returns the maximum possible frequency of any element after performing at most k
    unit‑increase or unit‑decrease operations on the array `nums`.

    turned into the same value (the median of that subset) with total cost
    sum(|num - median|) <= k.

    The algorithm:
    1. Sort the array.
    2. Pre‑compute prefix sums for O(1) range‑sum queries.
    3. Use a sliding window [l, r] (both inclusive). For each r we move l forward
       while the cost to bring the current window to its median exceeds k.
       The cost for a window is computed using the prefix sums:
           cost = median * (#elements left of median) - sum(left side) +
                  sum(right side) - median * (#elements right of median)

    Complexity: O(n log n) time for sorting, O(n) afterwards; O(n) extra space.

    for i, v in enumerate(nums):
```

```
        # first empty cell (row major order)
        for pos from 0 to H*W-1:
                if ((mask >> pos) & 1) == 0:
                        first = pos
                        break
        r = first // W
        c = first %  W

        # try every still unused tile
        for i, tid in enumerate(remaining_tiles):
                for (h, w) in orient[tid]:
                        # does the rectangle fit into the board?
                        if r + h > H or c + w > W:
                                continue

                        # build the mask of the cells that would be covered
                        new_mask = 0
                        ok = True
                        for dr in range(h):
                                row_start = (r + dr) * W + c          # first bit of this row
                                row_bits   = ((1 << w) - 1) << row_start
                                if row_bits & mask:                  # overlap ?
                                        ok = False
                                        break
                                new_mask |= row_bits
                        if not ok:
                                continue

                        # recurse with this tile placed
                        nxt = remaining_tiles[:i] + remaining_tiles[i+1:]
                        if dfs(mask | new_mask, nxt):
                                return True
        return False
```

#### 5.  Correctness Proof  

We prove that the algorithm prints **Yes** iff the board can be tiled.

---

##### Lemma 1  
If a placement of a subset of tiles covers the whole board,
there exists another placement of the *same* subset that also covers the board
and whose first placed tile has its upper‑left corner on the first empty cell
(scanning row‑major order) of the still empty board.

**Proof.**  
Take any correct placement. Scan the board row major until the first cell `p`
that belongs to some tile `T`. Move `T` (without rotation) so that its
upper‑left corner coincides with `p`. Because `p` was the first uncovered cell,
all cells above `p` and left of `p` are still empty, therefore the moved tile
still lies completely inside the board and does not intersect any other tile.
Thus we obtain another correct placement where the first placed tile starts at
the first empty cell. ∎



##### Lemma 2  
During `dfs(mask, remaining)` the recursive call
`dfs(mask | new_mask, remaining\{t})` is executed **iff** there exists a placement
of tile `t` (with one of its allowed orientations) whose upper‑left corner is
the first empty cell of `mask` and which does not overlap already occupied cells.

**Proof.**  
The function enumerates exactly all orientations of `t`.  
For each orientation it checks the board borders (`r+h ≤ H`, `c+w ≤ W`) and
whether any of the cells of the candidate rectangle intersect the current mask.
If both tests succeed the rectangle fits without overlap, `new_mask` is precisely
the set of its cells and the recursive call is performed.
Conversely, any placement of `t` whose upper‑left corner is the first empty cell
must satisfy those two tests, consequently the algorithm will examine it and
make the recursive call. ∎



##### Lemma 3  
`dfs(mask, R)` returns `True` **iff** the currently empty cells (those not set in
`mask`) can be perfectly tiled by the tiles in `R`.

**Proof.**  
*Soundness* (`True` ⇒ tiling exists).  
Induction on the number of empty cells.  
Base: `mask == FULL` ⇒ no empty cells ⇒ trivially tiled.  
Induction step: `mask != FULL`.  
`dfs` picks the first empty cell `p`. Because it finally returns `True`,
there exists a tile `t ∈ R` and an orientation such that the recursive call
`dfs(mask', R\{t})` (with `mask' = mask ∪ cells(t)`) returns `True`.  
By induction hypothesis the remaining empty cells can be tiled by `R\{t}`.
Together with `t` (which covers `p` and does not overlap) we obtain a tiling
of all empty cells.

*Completeness* (tiling exists ⇒ `True`).  
Assume a tiling of the empty cells by the tiles in `R` exists.
Consider the tile that covers the first empty cell `p`.  
By Lemma 1 we may assume that its upper‑left corner is exactly `p`.  
Lemma 2 tells us that `dfs` will try exactly this tile/orientation
and will recursively call `dfs` with the updated mask and the remaining tiles.
The rest of the tiling gives a recursive proof that the deeper call returns
`True`; therefore the current call also returns `True`. ∎



##### Lemma 4  
For a subset `S` whose total area equals `H·W`,
`dfs(0, S)` returns `True` **iff** the whole board can be tiled using exactly the
tiles of `S`.

**Proof.**  
Initially `mask = 0` (no cell occupied) and the empty cells are the whole board.
Apply Lemma 3 with `R = S`. ∎



##### Lemma 5  
If the algorithm prints **Yes**, a valid tiling exists.

**Proof.**  
The algorithm prints **Yes** only after it finds a subset `S`
with area `H·W` for which `dfs(0, S)` returns `True`.  
By Lemma 4 this implies that the board can be tiled with the tiles of `S`,
hence a valid tiling exists (unused tiles are simply the tiles not in `S`). ∎



##### Lemma 6  
If a valid tiling exists, the algorithm prints **Yes**.

**Proof.**  
Let `S` be the set of tiles actually used in the tiling.
Their total area is `H·W`, therefore the outer loop will examine exactly this
subset `S`.  
By Lemma 4 `dfs(0, S)` returns `True`, consequently the algorithm prints
**Yes**. ∎



##### Theorem  
The program outputs **Yes** iff it is possible to place some of the given tiles
on the `H × W` board so that every cell is covered by exactly one tile.

**Proof.**  
Directly from Lemma 5 (soundness) and Lemma 6 (completeness). ∎

#### 6.  Complexity Analysis  

*Number of subsets* : `2ⁿ ≤ 128`  

For one subset  

*Depth of recursion* ≤ size of subset ≤ 7  

*Branching factor* : at most  

`remaining tiles` · `2` orientations ≤ `7·2 = 14`  

Each placement tests at most `h·w ≤ 100` cells, but the implementation uses
bit operations on whole rows, i.e. `O(h)` integer operations.

Upper bound for one subset:

```
O( 7! · 2⁷ )   <   10⁴   recursive calls
```

Overall running time is far below one millisecond; memory consumption is
`O(1)` besides the recursion stack (depth ≤ 7).

```python
import sys

def solve() -> None:
    data = sys.stdin.read().strip().split()
    if not data:
        return
    it = iter(data)
    N = int(next(it))
    H = int(next(it))
    W = int(next(it))

    tiles = []
    for _ in range(N):
        a = int(next(it))
        b = int(next(it))
        tiles.append((a, b))

    total_cells = H * W
    FULL = (1 << total_cells) - 1

    # orientations for each tile (list of (h,w), duplicates removed)
    orient = []
    for a, b in tiles:
        o = [(a, b)]
        if a != b:
            o.append((b, a))
        orient.append(o)

    # ---------- recursive packer ----------
    sys.setrecursionlimit(10000)

    def dfs(mask: int, remaining: list) -> bool:
        """return True iff the empty cells can be tiled by the tiles in `remaining`"""
        if mask == FULL:
            return True

        # first empty cell (row major)
        pos = 0
        while (mask >> pos) & 1:
            pos += 1
        r = pos // W
        c = pos % W

        # try every remaining tile
        for i, tid in enumerate(remaining):
            for h, w in orient[tid]:
                if r + h > H or c + w > W:
                    continue
                # build mask of this placement
                new_mask = 0
                ok = True
                for dr in range(h):
                    row_start = (r + dr) * W + c
                    row_bits = ((1 << w) - 1) << row_start
                    if row_bits & mask:           # overlap
                        ok = False
                        break
                    new_mask |= row_bits
                if not ok:
                    continue
                nxt = remaining[:i] + remaining[i+1:]
                if dfs(mask | new_mask, nxt):
                    return True
        return False

    # ---------- enumerate subsets ----------
    answer = "No"
    for subset in range(1, 1 << N):
        # area of this subset
        area = 0
        for i in range(N):
            if (subset >> i) & 1:
                area += tiles[i][0] * tiles[i][1]
        if area != total_cells:
            continue

        # list of indices belonging to the subset, sorted by decreasing area
        idxs = [i for i in range(N) if (subset >> i) & 1]
        idxs.sort(key=lambda i: -tiles[i][0] * tiles[i][1])

        if dfs(0, idxs):
            answer = "Yes"
            break

    print(answer)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    solve()
```

```python
def findRepeatingAndMissing(grid):
    """
    Finds the number that appears twice and the number that is missing in an n x n matrix
    containing all numbers from 1 to n^2 exactly once, except one repeated and one missing.

    Parameters
    ----------
    grid : List[List[int]]
        A 2‑D list representing the matrix.

    Returns
    -------
    List[int]
        A list [a, b] where a is the repeated number and b is the missing number.

    n = len(grid)
    total = n * n

    # Frequency array for numbers 1..total
    freq = [0] * (total + 1)   # index 0 unused

    for row in grid:
        for val in row:
            freq[val] += 1

    repeated = missing = None
    for num in range(1, total + 1):
        if freq[num] == 2:
            repeated = num
        elif freq[num] == 0:
            missing = num

    # According to problem guarantees both will be found
    return [repeated, missing]
```

```python
def getSmallestString(s: str, k: int) -> str:
    if k == 0:
        return s
    
    result = []
    remaining_k = k
    
    for char in s:
        if remaining_k == 0:
            result.append(char)
            continue
            
        # Current character's position (0 for 'a', 25 for 'z')
        current_pos = ord(char) - ord('a')
        
        # Distance to 'a' in cyclic manner
        # Option 1: go forward from current to 'a'
        # Option 2: go backward from current to 'a' (through 'z')
        dist_to_a = min(current_pos, 26 - current_pos)
        
        if dist_to_a <= remaining_k:
            # We can change this character to 'a'
            result.append('a')
            remaining_k -= dist_to_a
        else:
            # We can't reach 'a', so we move as close as possible
            # We can move remaining_k steps toward 'a'
            if current_pos <= 13:  # It's closer to go backward
                new_pos = current_pos - remaining_k
            else:  # It's closer to go forward (through 'z')
                new_pos = current_pos + remaining_k
                if new_pos >= 26:
                    new_pos -= 26
                    
            result.append(chr(ord('a') + new_pos))
            remaining_k = 0
    
    return ''.join(result)
```

**Solution Explanation**

For every land cell we may assume that Takahashi crashed there.
From this start we follow the given moves `T`.

```
          L   : (i , j) → (i , j-1)
          R   : (i , j) → (i , j+1)
          U   : (i , j) → (i-1, j)
          D   : (i , j) → (i+1, j)
```

If at any step the new cell is sea (`'#'`) the assumption is impossible,
otherwise after the last move we obtain a *current* cell.
All different current cells obtained from at least one feasible start have
to be counted.

The outer border of the grid is guaranteed to be sea, therefore a move
never leaves the rectangular array – the first sea cell is always inside
the array and the program never accesses an illegal index.



--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### Algorithm
```
read H, W, N
read string T
read the H rows of the map into grid[0 … H-1][0 … W-1]

direction = { 'L': (0,-1), 'R': (0,1), 'U': (-1,0), 'D': (1,0) }

ans_set = empty set of pairs (row, col)

for every cell (r, c)                     // O(H·W)
        if grid[r][c] == '#': continue    // only land can be the start

        x, y = r, c
        ok = True
        for ch in T:                      // O(N)
                dx, dy = direction[ch]
                x += dx
                y += dy
                if grid[x][y] == '#':    // stepped on sea → impossible
                        ok = False
                        break
        if ok:                            // whole path stayed on land
                ans_set.add( (x, y) )    // (x,y) is the current cell

print size of ans_set
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### Correctness Proof  

We prove that the algorithm outputs exactly the number of cells that can be
Takahashi’s current position.

---

##### Lemma 1  
For a fixed start cell `s`, the algorithm declares `s` *feasible*
(`ok = True`) **iff** every cell on the path starting from `s`
and following `T` is land.

**Proof.**  
The algorithm simulates the moves step by step.
After each move it checks `grid[x][y]`.  
*If* a sea cell is encountered, `ok` becomes `False` and the simulation
stops – the path is not completely on land.  
*If* the simulation finishes without finding sea, each visited cell was
checked and was land, therefore the whole path is on land. ∎



##### Lemma 2  
If a start cell `s` is feasible, the algorithm adds exactly the cell that
is reached after performing all moves of `T` from `s` to the answer set.

**Proof.**  
When `ok` stays `True`, after the last iteration of the inner loop the
variables `(x, y)` hold the coordinates after executing the whole string
`T`. The algorithm inserts this pair into `ans_set`. No other cell is
inserted for this start. ∎



##### Lemma 3  
For every cell `c` that can be Takahashi’s current position,
`c` belongs to `ans_set` after the algorithm finishes.

**Proof.**  
If `c` can be the current position, there exists at least one start cell
`s` such that the whole path from `s` stays on land and ends at `c`.
By Lemma 1 the algorithm will mark `s` feasible,
by Lemma 2 it will insert the ending cell of that simulation,
which is exactly `c`, into `ans_set`. ∎



##### Lemma 4  
Every cell stored in `ans_set` can be Takahashi’s current position.

**Proof.**  
A cell `c` is inserted only after some start `s` was processed,
the inner loop finished without meeting sea and therefore, by Lemma 1,
the whole path from `s` is on land.
Consequently `c` is the true end of a valid path and can be the current
position. ∎



##### Theorem  
The number printed by the algorithm equals the number of cells that could
be Takahashi’s current position.

**Proof.**  
By Lemma 3 every possible current cell belongs to `ans_set`
(so `ans_set` is a superset of the desired set).  
By Lemma 4 every element of `ans_set` is a possible current cell
(so `ans_set` is a subset of the desired set).  
Thus the two sets are identical, and their cardinalities are equal.
The algorithm prints the cardinality, therefore the output is correct. ∎



--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### Complexity Analysis  

*Outer loop* — at most `H·W ≤ 500·500 = 250 000` iterations.  
*Inner loop* — at most `N ≤ 500` steps, but it stops earlier when sea is
met.

Worst‑case time: `O(H·W·N) ≤ 125 000 000` elementary operations,
easily fast enough in Python (simple integer arithmetic and array look‑ups).

Memory consumption: the grid (`H·W` characters) and a set of at most
`H·W` pairs → `O(H·W)` ≤ 250 k entries, well within limits.

```python
    H, W, N = map(int, next(it).split())
    T = next(it).strip()

    # direction vectors
    d = {
        'L': (0, -1),
        'R': (0, 1),
```

Question: a 12 meter long wire is cut into two pieces . if the longer piece is then used to form a perimeter of a square , what is the probability that the area of the square will be more than 4 if the original wire was cut at an arbitrary point ?

Options: 
A. 1 / 6
B. 2 / 3
C. 3 / 10
D. 1 / 3
E. 2 / 5

generated_result.generated_answer:
Let the cut be made at a point $ x $ meters from one end, where $ 0 < x < 12 $. The two pieces are $ x $ and $ 12 - x $; assume without loss of generality that the longer piece is used, so we take $ \max(x, 12 - x) $. This longer piece forms the perimeter of a square, so its side is $ \frac{\text{longer piece}}{4} $, and the area is $ \left(\frac{\text{longer piece}}{4}\right)^2 $. We want the area $ > 4 $, so:

$$
\left(\frac{L}{4}\right)^2 > 4 \Rightarrow \frac{L^2}{16} > 4 \Rightarrow L^2 > 64 \Rightarrow L > 8
$$

So the longer piece must be greater than 8 meters. Since the total length is 12, the longer piece exceeds 8 when the cut is made such that either $ x > 8 $ or $ 12 - x > 8 $ (i.e., $ x < 4 $). So the favorable region is $ x \in (0, 4) \cup (8, 12) $, which has total length $ 4 + 4 = 8 $. The total possible cut points are over 12 meters, so the probability is:

$$
\frac{8}{12} = \frac{2}{3}
$$

\boxed{B}

Context:  In Rome, in the 1980s, famous Italian film director Salvatore Di Vita returns home late one evening, where his girlfriend sleepily tells him that his mother called to say someone named Alfredo has died. Salvatore obviously shies from committed relationships and has not been to his home village of Giancaldo, Sicily in 30 years. As his girlfriend asks him who Alfredo is, Salvatore flashes back to his childhood.
It is a few years after World War II. Six-year-old Salvatore is the mischievous, intelligent son of a war widow. Nicknamed Toto, he discovers a love for films and spends every free moment at the movie house Cinema Paradiso. Although they initially start off on tense terms, he develops a friendship with the fatherly projectionist, Alfredo, who takes a shine to the young boy and often lets him watch movies from the projection booth. During the shows, the audience can be heard booing when there are missing sections, causing the films to suddenly jump, bypassing a critical romantic kiss or embrace. The local priest had ordered these sections censored, and the deleted scenes are piled on the projection room floor. At first, Alfredo considers Toto a bit of a pest, but eventually he teaches Salvatore to operate the film projector.
The montage ends as the movie house catches fire (highly flammable nitrate film was in routine use at the time) as Alfredo was projecting The Firemen of Viggiù after hours, on the wall of a nearby house. Salvatore saves Alfredo's life, but not before some film reels explode in Alfredo's face, leaving him permanently blind. The Cinema Paradiso is rebuilt by a town citizen, Ciccio, who invests his football lottery winnings. Salvatore, still a child, is hired as the new projectionist, as he is the only person who knows how to run the machines.
About a decade later, Salvatore, now in high school, is still operating the projector at the Cinema Paradiso. His relationship with the blind Alfredo has strengthened, and Salvatore often looks to him for help — advice that Alfredo often dispenses by quoting classic films. Salvatore has been experimenting with film, using a home movie camera, and he has met, and captured on film, Elena, daughter of a wealthy banker. Salvatore woos — and wins — Elena's heart, only to lose her due to her father's disapproval.
As Elena and her family move away, Salvatore leaves town for compulsory military service. His attempts to write to Elena are fruitless; his letters are returned as undeliverable. Upon his return from the military, Alfredo urges Salvatore to leave Giancaldo permanently, counseling that the town is too small for Salvatore to ever find his dreams. Moreover, the old man tells him, once Salvatore leaves, he must pursue his destiny wholeheartedly, never looking back and never returning, even to visit; he must never give in to nostalgia or even write or think about them. They tearfully embrace, and Salvatore leaves town to pursue his future, as a filmmaker.
Salvatore has obeyed Alfredo, but he returns home to attend the funeral. Though the town has changed greatly, he now understands why Alfredo thought it was important that he leave. Alfredo's widow tells him that the old man followed Salvatore's successes with pride, and he left him something — an unlabeled film reel and the old stool that Salvatore once stood on to operate the projector. Salvatore learns that Cinema Paradiso is to be demolished to make way for a parking lot. At the funeral, he recognizes the faces of many people who attended the cinema when he was the projectionist.
Salvatore returns to Rome. He watches Alfredo's reel and discovers that it comprises a very special montage. It contains all of the romantic scenes the priest had ordered cut from movies; Alfredo had spliced the sequences together to form a single film. Salvatore has made peace with his past.

He uses this notably in The Thirty Nine Steps. The novel contrasts the domestic characters, heroes and villains, with their more alien Russian counterparts. Huntingtower is characteristic of Buchan’s novels, particularly in its class-based paternalism; its xenophobic prejudices, which are mitigated by instinctive humanity and dry humour; and its shrewd common-sense understanding of personality and motivation. We see Buchan's class based paternalism in the attitudes of various characters, from Saskia's insistence on pointing out the former status of her Russian family to Phemie Morran's lifelong loyalty to the extinct Kennedy family, to whom she was once a domestic servant. Heritage and McCunn instantly react to the first foreign resident of Huntingtower, a man called Leon, whose unwholesome appearance Buchan describes with relish:
"He was a sturdy fellow in a suit of blackclothes which had not been made for him. He might have been a butler en deshabille, but for the presence of a pair of field boots into which he had tucked the ends of his trousers. The curious thing about him was his face, which was decorated with features so tiny as to give the impression of a monstrous child. Each in itself was well enough formed, but eyes, nose, mouth, chin were of smallness curiously out of proportion to the head and body. Such an anomaly might have been redeemed by the expression; good-humour would have invested it with an air of agreeable farce. But there was no friendliness in the man’s face. It was set like a judge’s in a stony impassiveness." Huntingtower chapter three.
The moment when Dickson McCunn relinquishes his timid wish to remain strictly inside the law and decides to take a hand against the foreign conspirators gives an ironic insight into McCunn's social conditioning, whereby the veranda is an acceptable way to break into a house and the coal hole is unacceptable.
"They both looked at Dickson, and Dickson, scarlet in the face, looked back at them. He had suddenly found the thought of a solitary march to Auchenlochan intolerable. Once again he was at the parting of the ways, and once more caprice determined his decision. That the coal-hole was out of the question had worked a change in his views, Somehow it seemed to him less burglarious to enter by a veranda. He felt very frightened but for the moment quite resolute. “I’m coming with you,” he said." Huntingtower chapter five.
In this novel Buchan creates characters across a broad spectrum of Scottish social classes and backgrounds, and while no one except McCunn is presented in great depth, we are given sharp and revealing character sketches of other key characters. Heritage’s single handed defence of the actual tower and his attempt to free-climb away from the burning building show not only his actions but his reasons and thinking, why he is doing what he is doing. Wee Jaikie's inner life is only hinted at occasionally, but his dogged perseverance and resourcefulness come through at several moments when his interventions are important. In the final resolution of the story, a band of adventurers ranging from an injured laird and his faithful menservants to a group of semi-outcast street urchins from Glasgow have bonded and have combined to fight for a common purpose, out of belief in right and wrong, and allegiance to Scotland.

Context:  To Epicurus, the unhappiness and degradation of humans arose largely from the dread which they entertained of the power of the deities, from terror of their wrath. This wrath was supposed to be displayed by the misfortunes inflicted in this life and by the everlasting tortures that were the lot of the guilty in a future state (or, where these feelings were not strongly developed, from a vague dread of gloom and misery after death). To remove these fears, and thus to establish tranquility in the heart, was the purpose of his teaching. Thus the deities, whose existence he did not deny, lived forevermore in the enjoyment of absolute peace, strangers to all the passions, desires, and fears, which agitate the human heart, totally indifferent to the world and its inhabitants, unmoved alike by their virtues and their crimes.
To prove this position he called upon the atomism of Democritus, so as to demonstrate that the material universe was formed not by a Supreme Being, but by the mixing of elemental particles that had existed from all eternity governed by certain simple laws. Lucretius' task was to clearly state and fully develop these views in an attractive form; his work was an attempt to show that everything in nature can be explained by natural laws, without the need for the intervention of divine beings.
Lucretius identifies the supernatural with the notion that the deities created our world or interfere with its operations in some way. He argues against fear of such deities by demonstrating, through observations and arguments, that the operations of the world can be accounted for in terms of natural phenomena. These phenomena are the regular, but purposeless motions and interactions of tiny atoms in empty space. Meanwhile, he argues against the fear of death by stating that death is the dissipation of a being's material mind. Lucretius uses the analogy of a vessel, stating that the physical body is the vessel that holds both the mind (mens) and spirit (anima) of a human being. Neither the mind nor spirit can survive independent of the body. Thus Lucretius states that once the vessel (the body) shatters (dies) its contents (mind and spirit) can no longer exist. So, as a simple ceasing-to-be, death can be neither good nor bad for this being. Being completely devoid of sensation and thought, a dead person cannot miss being alive. According to Lucretius, fear of death is a projection of terrors experienced in life, of pain that only a living (intact) mind can feel. Lucretius also puts forward the 'symmetry argument' against the fear of death. In it, he says that people who fear the prospect of eternal non-existence after death should think back to the eternity of non-existence before their birth, which probably did not cause them much suffering.

generated_result.generated_answer:

This atomic theory underpins his argument that the deities do not intervene in the world.

\boxed{{Democritus}}

Context:  The galaxy is in the midst of a civil war. Spies for the Rebel Alliance have stolen plans to the Galactic Empire's Death Star, a heavily armed space station capable of destroying planets.
